prompts:
Use case: ui-mockup.
Create one exceptionally art-directed, high-fidelity desktop screen of an interactive history EXPERIENCE INSIDE an existing website, landscape 16:10 composition. This is a visual concept, not a verified historical map.
Input images 1, 2, 3 are STYLE AND QUALITY REFERENCES ONLY, not edit targets. Match their ambitious editorial composition, tactile atmosphere, large expressive typography, striking historical imagery, and interaction controls integrated into the scene. Do not copy their Cold War content, political iconography, or dark blue/red palette. This must look like a beautiful, usable digital museum exhibit, not a SaaS dashboard, landing page, screenshot of a flat poster, or generic cards.

Subject: "ROME: A WORLD CONNECTED". A learning scene about how maritime routes connected the Roman Mediterranean.
Art direction: luminous warm ivory and aged parchment, terracotta, lapis sea blue, restrained antique gold. Sophisticated archaeological atlas meets richly illustrated editorial feature. The dominant visual is a meticulously composed painterly aerial reconstruction of an ancient Mediterranean harbour: merchant vessels, quays, warehouses, distant hills, sunlight on water. It is explicitly captioned "Illustrated reconstruction". Blend this seamlessly into a beautiful stylized engraved map of the Mediterranean with subtle glowing route lines and a few readable port labels. A sophisticated tapestry of illustrative artwork and clear interactive layers, not a full-screen painting with tiny unreadable interface.

Composition: thin quiet website chrome, generous primary canvas, a narrow left chapter rail. Top header wordmark "HISTORY" left and small "Library", "Share", "Sources" controls right. Left chapter rail uses clear labels "01 The sea", "02 Trade", "03 Cities", "04 Connections", with "02 Trade" active. Main upper left a small overline "CHAPTER 02 / 04", massive elegant serif headline "AN EMPIRE\nIN MOTION", and a short two-sentence learning introduction: "Follow the routes that connected distant shores. Discover how goods, people, and ideas moved across the sea." Let typography have room.
The map/harbour illustration fills most of the center/right and the lower edge. Selectable warm gold port markers with one selected. A small integrated detail panel reads "OSTIA" and "A gateway to Rome", with a circular thumbnail of a ship and a readable "Explore this port →" control. Directly on the map, a restrained segmented control "Grain  |  Oil  |  Pottery" has Grain selected. Under it a small cue "Choose a cargo to reveal its journey". A single route is visually highlighted across the map rather than many tangled lines.
At bottom, an elegant time/navigation strip with "Replay journey", a short stage indicator, and "Continue: The city grows →". No bibliography within the art; sources are reached through the top Sources control and at the end of the full experience.
Constraints: one cohesive full-screen interface, readable hierarchy and large controls, striking real artistic richness comparable to references, illustrations large and integral to the experience, subtle textures away from small text, no confetti, no XP, no fake statistics, no tables, no three-column dashboard cards, no outer browser window or monitor, no watermarks. Mark "Concept study" unobtrusively in the bottom margin.

Use case: ui-mockup.
Create one exceptionally art-directed, high-fidelity desktop screen of an interactive history EXPERIENCE INSIDE an existing website, landscape 16:10 composition. This is a visual concept and its pictures are illustrative, not authenticated archival material.
Input images 1, 2, 3 are STYLE AND QUALITY REFERENCES ONLY, not edit targets. Match their ambitious cinematic editorial composition, tactile atmosphere, large expressive typography, historical collage, and controls integrated into the scene. Do not copy their Cold War content, Kennedy imagery, maps, or Soviet iconography. This must look like a beautiful usable interactive documentary, not a SaaS dashboard, landing page, screenshot of a flat poster, or generic card gallery. Visibly different visual direction from an ancient-history parchment atlas.

Subject: "THE RACE TO THE MOON". A dramatic mission-planning chapter illustrating the problem of reaching the Moon and returning, inviting exploration rather than a pretend predictive simulation.
Art direction: midnight ink, silver-white, warm amber mission annotation, a tiny accent of spacecraft orange; 1960s technical manuals, contact sheets, beautiful orbital linework, large photographic-style lunar and astronaut imagery, elegantly controlled grain. Images are ambitious and integral, not small decorative thumbnails.
Composition: quiet thin header "HISTORY" left, a breadcrumb "The race to the Moon", and compact "Library", "Share", "Sources" controls at right. Narrow chapter rail left with "01 The challenge", "02 The route", "03 The landing", "04 The return"; "02 The route" active.
At upper left of main content, small overline "CHAPTER 02 / 04", enormous condensed editorial headline "GET THERE.\nGET HOME.", followed by restrained readable text: "Reaching the Moon was only half the problem. Explore how mission planners connected the outward journey, landing, and return." Use beautiful typographic hierarchy, strong generous negative space.
The dominant right/central art is a huge beautifully lit crescent Moon with realistic crater relief, cutout-style lunar lander imagery, and delicate clear orbital paths joining a small Earth at lower left of the main canvas to the Moon. Small numbered stage markers make it clear where to click. "Concept illustration" in a small caption by the main image. Subtle blueprint sheets and a restrained photographic-style mission control contact strip frame the lower edge without harming legibility.
One opened integrated amber-edged panel "02 / LUNAR ORBIT" reads "Explore the rendezvous" with a compact schematic of two vehicles and a clear action "Trace the return path →". At bottom two or three beautifully integrated choice tabs "Outbound", "At the Moon", "Homeward", with "At the Moon" selected; don't use a three-card marketing layout. A short prompt says "Select a stage to follow the mission."
Bottom right clear "Continue: Choosing a landing site →"; bottom left a compact "Ask about this scene" affordance, not an open chat panel. No bibliography within the art; sources accessible through top control and at the end of the full experience.
Constraints: cohesive usable full-screen interface, striking editorial image composition comparable to provided references, large readable headline and labels, interaction mechanics visible, no invented mission statistics, no long paragraphs, no cluttered control panels or KPI boxes, no generic rounded cards, no outer browser window or monitor, no watermarks. Mark "Concept study" unobtrusively in bottom margin.
